references.text: The demand to let the people go free to serve the Lord is repeated several times through the plagues, first here.
Moses conveys the Lord's command to Pharaoh: 'Let my people go, so that they may serve me' - the same demand that the servants now urge Pharaoh to fulfill.
Repeated demand to let the people go to serve the Lord, which the servants refer to.
After the final plague, Pharaoh and the Egyptians finally realize that the land is destroyed, and they ask the Israelites to leave.
The warning that foreign gods will become a snare (mokesh) for Israel, the same word used here of Moses as a snare for Egypt.
The warning that idolatry will become a snare (mokesh), the same Hebrew word that the servants use about the situation.
Saul describes David as a snare (mokesh) to the Philistines, similar language used for someone who causes destruction.
Pharaoh admits his sin after the locust plague, confirming the servants' warning about Egypt's destruction.
The contrast between the servants' warning of ruin before liberation and their regret after the people have fled highlights Pharaoh's stubbornness and the consequences of opposing God's will.
The irony that Pharaoh's servants utter God's own command ('Let them go to serve') against their master confirms that God's word is unavoidable even in the enemy's camp.
The connection between the servants' current warning in 10:7 and their future submissive plea in 11:8 illustrates the gradual victory God's word achieves over Pharaoh's household.
The theme of Pharaoh's deceit ('deceive us again') in 8:25 is confirmed by the servants' description of him as a 'snare' in 10:7.
The identical wording from God's mouth (8:16) later repeated by Pharaoh's servants (10:7) shows how God's will breaks through even in the enemy's camp.
